quiz_metadata.title: Advanced Regression & Model Diagnostics
quiz_metadata.description: Practice quiz covering interaction terms, polynomial regression, multicollinearity, and VIF/correlation diagnostics.
quiz_metadata.author: Generated from quiz.txt

questions.section: Section 1: Interaction Terms & Sample Size
questions.question_text: Why do interaction terms typically require a larger sample size than simple main effects?
options: A) Interaction terms introduce non-linear parameters that violate OLS assumptions.
B) Interaction terms estimate subgroup or conditional effects, which drastically reduces the effective sample size for each comparison.
C) Interaction terms always create perfect multicollinearity in small samples.
D) Interaction terms double the variance of the error term ($\sigma^2$).
questions.explanation: Interaction terms evaluate conditional effects (subgroups), which drastically reduces statistical power and effective sample size compared to main effects.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 1: Interaction Terms & Sample Size
questions.question_text: When testing a two-way interaction between two continuous variables ($X_1 \cdot X_2$), statistical power is fundamentally constrained by:
options: A) The sum of the main effects.
B) The product of the variances of $X_1$ and $X_2$.
C) The residual variance and the reduced variation in the product term relative to main effects.
D) The intercept of the model.
questions.explanation: The product term has less independent variation than the main terms, leading to larger standard errors unless sample sizes are large.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 1: Interaction Terms & Sample Size
questions.question_text: In an experiment with a $2 \times 2$ factorial design, detecting a main effect of size $d$ requires a sample size $N$. Roughly how large a sample size is required to detect an interaction effect of the same magnitude ($d$)?
options: A) $N$
questions.explanation: Standard power calculations show that detecting an interaction of equal magnitude to a main effect typically requires at least 4 times the sample size.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 1: Interaction Terms & Sample Size
questions.question_text: What happens to the standard error of an interaction coefficient ($\beta_3$) as sample size ($n$) decreases?
options: A) It decreases proportionally.
B) It increases, leading to wider confidence intervals and lower statistical power (higher Type II error rate).
C) It remains unchanged because standard error depends only on $\sigma^2$.
D) It becomes zero when $n < 30$.
questions.explanation: Smaller sample sizes lead to higher standard errors ($\text{SE}(\hat{\beta}) \propto 1/\sqrt{n}$).
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 1: Interaction Terms & Sample Size
questions.question_text: Why does high correlation between main effect terms ($X_1$ and $X_2$) and their product term ($X_1 X_2$) increase sample size requirements?
options: A) It inflates the variance of the estimated interaction coefficient, requiring more data to achieve precise estimates.
B) It makes it mathematically impossible to calculate $R^2$.
C) It forces the model to use logistic regression instead of linear regression.
D) It biases the coefficient estimates toward zero.
questions.explanation: High correlation inflates variance, requiring more observations to lower standard errors back down to acceptable levels.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 1: Interaction Terms & Sample Size
questions.question_text: If a study is powered at 80% to detect main effects, its statistical power to detect a cross-over interaction of the same effect size is generally:
options: A) Much higher (near 95%)
B) Identical (80%)
C) Substantially lower (often around 20–50% depending on sample design)
questions.explanation: Power drops significantly for interactions because variance for product terms is higher.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 2: Polynomial Terms & Multicollinearity
questions.question_text: Why do polynomial terms (e.g., $X, X^2, X^3$) inherently tend to produce multicollinearity?
options: A) Higher-order powers of positive numbers naturally correlate strongly with the original variable unless centered.
B) Polynomial terms violate the homoscedasticity assumption.
C) Exponents change the measurement units of the variable unpredictably.
D) Polynomial terms cause the dependent variable $Y$ to become non-normal.
questions.explanation: Taking powers of positive numbers naturally preserves monotonic ordering, creating high linear correlation between $X$ and $X^k$.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 2: Polynomial Terms & Multicollinearity
questions.question_text: In which of the following scenarios will polynomial terms generate severe structural multicollinearity?
options: A) When $X$ is mean-centered before squaring ($X_{centered} = X - \bar{X}$).
B) When $X$ consists strictly of positive values far away from zero (e.g., age ranging from 40 to 80).
C) When $X$ is symmetrically distributed around zero (e.g., values from $-10$ to $+10$).
D) When the sample size is greater than $1,000$.
questions.explanation: When values are strictly positive and far from zero, $X$ and $X^2$ track each other almost linearly.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 2: Polynomial Terms & Multicollinearity
questions.question_text: What simple transformation mitigates structural multicollinearity between a main effect $X$ and its polynomial $X^2$?
options: A) Log-transforming the dependent variable $Y$.
B) Mean-centering the predictor variable $X$ before raising it to powers.
C) Multiplying $X$ by a constant $k$.
D) Dividing $X$ by the standard deviation of $Y$.
questions.explanation: Mean-centering places the origin at the mean, making $X$ and $X^2$ orthogonal or nearly orthogonal if $X$ is symmetric.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 2: Polynomial Terms & Multicollinearity
questions.question_text: What is the difference between "structural multicollinearity" and "data-based multicollinearity" in polynomial regression?
options: A) Structural multicollinearity is caused by creating mathematical functions (powers) of variables; data-based is inherent to relationships between distinct predictors in the population.
B) Data-based multicollinearity can be fixed by mean-centering; structural multicollinearity cannot.
C) Structural multicollinearity biases $R^2$; data-based multicollinearity does not.
D) There is no functional difference; the terms are interchangeable synonyms for heteroscedasticity.
questions.explanation: Structural multicollinearity is an artifact of model creation ($X^2, X_1 X_2$); data-based is inherent in raw data relationships.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 2: Polynomial Terms & Multicollinearity
questions.question_text: If $X$ ranges strictly from $100$ to $150$, what is the expected relationship between $X$ and $X^2$?
options: A) Zero correlation ($r = 0$).
B) Perfect negative correlation ($r = -1.0$).
C) Extremely high positive correlation ($r \approx 0.98+$).
D) Non-monotonic relationship.
questions.explanation: Squaring numbers in a range far above zero generates an almost perfectly correlated straight curve over that interval.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 2: Polynomial Terms & Multicollinearity
questions.question_text: Does high structural multicollinearity between $X$ and $X^2$ invalidate the overall model's predictions ($\hat{Y}$)?
options: A) Yes, the predicted values become entirely uninterpretable.
B) No, overall model fit and predictions remain unaffected; only the individual coefficient standard errors and interpretability are impacted.
C) Yes, it introduces severe bias into the $F$-statistic.
D) Only if $R^2 < 0.50$.
questions.explanation: Multicollinearity inflates standard errors of individual coefficients, but overall model fit ($R^2$, overall predictions) remains unbiased and valid.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 3: Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) vs. Correlation Matrix
questions.question_text: Why is a bivariate correlation matrix insufficient for detecting multicollinearity in a model with three or more predictors ($X_1, X_2, X_3$)?
options: A) Correlation matrices only evaluate linear relationships between two variables at a time, missing complex linear combinations among multiple variables.
B) Bivariate correlation cannot be calculated for continuous variables.
C) Correlation values are capped at $0.50$ in multiple regression.
D) Correlation matrices do not report $p$-values.
questions.explanation: High linear combinations among 3+ variables (e.g., $X_1 \approx X_2 + X_3$) can exist even if all pairwise correlations are low ($r < 0.30$).
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 3: Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) vs. Correlation Matrix
questions.question_text: How is the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for a predictor $X_j$ calculated?
options: A) $\text{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{r_{y, x_j}}$
B) $\text{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{1 - R_j^2}$, where $R_j^2$ is the coefficient of determination from regressing $X_j$ on all other predictors.
C) $\text{VIF}_j = \frac{\text{Var}(Y)}{\text{Var}(X_j)}$
D) $\text{VIF}_j = 1 + R_{overall}^2$
questions.explanation: Standard mathematical definition of Variance Inflation Factor.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 3: Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) vs. Correlation Matrix
questions.question_text: A VIF value of $1.0$ indicates:
options: A) Perfect collinearity between $X_j$ and other predictors.
B) That $X_j$ explains 100% of the variance in $Y$.
C) Complete absence of linear correlation between $X_j$ and all other predictors in the model.
D) That the standard error of the coefficient is inflated by a factor of 10.
questions.explanation: $\text{VIF} = 1 / (1 - 0) = 1.0$, indicating zero correlation with other predictors in the model.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 3: Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) vs. Correlation Matrix
questions.question_text: If three predictors ($X_1, X_2, X_3$) collectively predict $X_4$ with an $R_4^2 = 0.90$, what is the VIF for $X_4$?
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 3: Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) vs. Correlation Matrix
questions.question_text: What standard threshold for VIF is most commonly cited as indicating problematic multicollinearity requiring remediation?
options: A) $\text{VIF} > 1.0$
B) $\text{VIF} > 2.0$
C) $\text{VIF} > 5 \text{ or } 10$
D) $\text{VIF} > 100$
questions.explanation: A VIF exceeding 5 or 10 is standard convention for problematic collinearity.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 3: Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) vs. Correlation Matrix
questions.question_text: Multicollinearity driven by a combination of predictors (e.g., $X_1 \approx X_2 + X_3$) where no single pairwise correlation exceeds $0.30$ is known as:
options: A) Pairwise collinearity.
B) Multicollinear homoscedasticity.
C) Multicollinearity due to linear dependence (or hyper-planar collinearity).
D) Non-linear endogeneity.
questions.explanation: Linear combination/dependence across multiple dimensions.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 3: Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) vs. Correlation Matrix
questions.question_text: What does a VIF of $4.0$ mean for the standard error of a coefficient?
options: A) The standard error is $4$ times larger than it would be if the predictor were uncorrelated with other predictors.
B) The standard error is $\sqrt{4} = 2$ times larger than it would be if the predictor were uncorrelated with other predictors.
C) The variance of the error term is multiplied by $4$.
D) The confidence interval is $16$ times wider.
questions.explanation: $\text{SE}$ inflation factor is $\sqrt{\text{VIF}} = \sqrt{4} = 2$.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 4: Why/When to Use Correlation Instead of VIF
questions.question_text: Under which condition is a pairwise correlation matrix preferred over VIF for diagnosing data issues?
options: A) During initial Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) prior to model specification, to quickly spot direct pairwise redundancies.
B) When assessing multicollinearity among 20+ mutually orthogonal predictors.
C) When calculating interaction terms between non-centered continuous variables.
D) When fitting non-linear neural networks.
questions.explanation: Correlation matrices are simple, fast, and intuitive tools for initial pre-modeling feature inspection.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 4: Why/When to Use Correlation Instead of VIF
questions.question_text: Why might an investigator rely on pairwise correlations rather than VIF when screening a massive dataset with thousands of features ($p \gg n$)?
options: A) VIF cannot be calculated computationally when $p > n$ because the design matrix is not invertible.
B) Correlation values are always more accurate than VIF.
C) Correlation eliminates the need for cross-validation.
D) VIF requires normal distributions, whereas correlation does not.
questions.explanation: Regressing each variable on all others when $p > n$ causes matrix non-invertibility (overdetermined system), making standard VIF calculation impossible.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 4: Why/When to Use Correlation Instead of VIF
questions.question_text: What is a major conceptual limitation of VIF compared to a correlation matrix?
options: A) VIF cannot detect collinearity between two predictors.
B) VIF gives an aggregate score for a predictor against all others, but does not explicitly show *which specific pair* of variables is causing the collinearity.
C) VIF is bounded between $-1$ and $+1$.
D) VIF depends on the scale of the dependent variable $Y$.
questions.explanation: VIF tells you *that* a variable is collinear with the rest of the model, but not *which specific other variable(s)* it is collinear with.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 4: Why/When to Use Correlation Instead of VIF
questions.question_text: If two variables ($X_1$ and $X_2$) have a pairwise correlation of $r = 0.95$, what does this tell you that a VIF value alone does not?
options: A) The exact direction (positive or negative) and specific identity of the collinear pair.
B) The exact inflation factor of the coefficient's variance.
C) The proportion of variance explained in $Y$.
D) Whether the model satisfies linear regression assumptions.
questions.explanation: Pairwise correlation explicitly reveals the sign ($+$ or $-$) and pinpoints the exact pair of variables involved.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 4: Why/When to Use Correlation Instead of VIF
questions.question_text: In screening for bivariate non-linear patterns or preliminary data cleaning, correlation matrices (and visual scatterplot matrices) are superior to VIF because VIF:
options: A) Only measures total linear predictability ($R_j^2$) of one feature from a set of features in a specified model structure.
B) Is an unstable statistic in sample sizes over 100.
C) Automatically removes non-linear patterns.
D) Can only be computed for categorical predictors.
questions.explanation: VIF summarizes multiple linear regression $R^2$; scatterplots and correlation matrices allow pair-by-pair examination.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.

questions.section: Section 4: Why/When to Use Correlation Instead of VIF
questions.question_text: Which diagnostic tool combination represents best practice when building a multiple linear regression model with potential collinearity issues?
options: A) Relying solely on $R^2$ and $p$-values.
B) Inspecting bivariate correlations/plots during initial feature screening, followed by evaluating VIFs once the multiple regression model is specified.
C) Using VIF for simple linear regression and correlation matrices for multiple regression.
D) Ignoring both unless the $F$-statistic is non-significant.
questions.explanation: Using correlation/plots first for data cleaning, then VIF for multiple regression diagnostics is standard statistical practice.
questions.learning_objective: Apply regression concepts and diagnostics to interpret model behavior.
